chapter_title: Paul at Ephesus, Part 2: Ideas, Legacy, and Lessons in Leading Change
learning_objective: The learner will organize twelve dated events from 386 CE to 1999 into four strands of Paul's later influence (grace and faith; conscience and equality; contempt and its repudiation; rereading Paul), placing at least 10 of 12 in the correct strand.
specification:
Type: timeline **sim-id:** how-pauls-words-traveled
**Library:** vis-timeline
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Analyze
**Bloom Verb:** organize
**Learning Objective:** The learner will organize twelve dated events from 386 CE to 1999 into four strands of Paul's later influence (grace and faith; conscience and equality; contempt and its repudiation; rereading Paul), placing at least 10 of 12 in the correct strand. **Prerequisites:** grace and faith, individual conscience, the idea of human equality, Christian anti-Judaism, the New Perspective on Paul, Augustine of Hippo, the Protestant Reformation (all defined in the chapter above this block). **Evidence of Mastery:** The learner drags each of 12 event cards into one of four horizontal strands on the timeline. The card's date is fixed; only its strand is chosen. A placement is correct when it matches the "Correct strand" column in Content. Mastery is 10 of 12 correct on the first Check. Reading event details is exploration, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) Paul's influence ran in one direction, either all good or all harmful. (2) Each historical figure belongs to one strand; in fact Luther appears in three. (3) Scholarly rereading of Paul is a recent fad with no history; it began in the 1960s and 1970s. (4) The Reformation was about conscience alone; its starting point was grace. **Instructional Rationale:** Organizing events into strands is an Analyze task: the learner must break each event down to the Pauline idea it carried. Seeing one figure, Luther, land in three strands makes the contested legacy concrete in a way a single narrative cannot. **Content:** Strands, with the definition shown on each: - **Grace and faith:** events in which Paul's teaching that people are put right with God by grace, through faith, was received or argued over. - **Conscience and equality:** events in which Paul's words were used for, or against, individual conscience or the equal worth of people. - **Contempt and its repudiation:** events in Christian treatment of Jews that drew on, or later corrected, readings of Paul. - **Rereading Paul:** scholarly work that changed how Paul is read. Event cards, in this fixed order: | # | Date | Event shown to the learner | Correct strand | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | 386 CE | Augustine reads Romans 13 in a garden in Milan and ends his indecision | Grace and faith | His conversion through Paul shaped his later teaching that grace comes first. | | 2 | c. 386–387 CE | John Chrysostom preaches eight sermons in Antioch against Christians who attend synagogue festivals | Contempt and its repudiation | The sermons are a classic of anti-Jewish preaching. | | 3 | 1517 | Luther issues the 95 Theses against the sale of indulgences | Grace and faith | His protest grew from his reading of Romans: righteousness is a gift, not something bought or earned. | | 4 | 1521 | Luther tells the Diet of Worms his conscience is captive to the Word of God | Conscience and equality | A founding moment for the idea that conscience must not be forced. | | 5 | 1543 | Luther publishes *On the Jews and Their Lies* | Contempt and its repudiation | The tract urged burning synagogues and was later reprinted by the Nazis. | | 6 | 1738 | John Wesley hears Luther's preface to Romans read and feels his heart "strangely warmed" | Grace and faith | Romans, read through Luther, started the Methodist movement. | | 7 | 1807 | A *Slave Bible* printed in London for the British West Indies leaves out Galatians 3:28 | Conscience and equality | Removing "no longer slave or free" shows that slaveholders feared the verse's power. | | 8 | 1963 | Krister Stendahl argues that the West read its own anxious conscience into Paul | Rereading Paul | A scholarly correction of the Augustine-to-Luther reading. | | 9 | 1965 | *Nostra Aetate* says Jews must not be presented as rejected or accursed by God, quoting Romans 11 | Contempt and its repudiation | The Catholic Church repudiated the teaching of contempt, using Paul's own words. | | 10 | 1977 | E. P. Sanders shows that the Judaism of Paul's day was not a religion of earning salvation | Rereading Paul | His work launched the "New Perspective on Paul." | | 11 | 1982 | James Dunn names the "New Perspective on Paul" in a lecture | Rereading Paul | He read "works of the law" as the markers that separated Jews from Gentiles. | | 12 | 1999 | Lutherans and Catholics sign a *Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification* | Grace and faith | It stated a shared understanding of the question that split the Western church in the 1500s. | Answer counts: Grace and faith 4, Conscience and equality 2, Contempt and its repudiation 3, Rereading Paul 3. **Provenance:** Events, dates, and strands come from this chapter's sections "Grace and Faith," "Augustine of Hippo," "The Protestant Reformation," "Individual Conscience," "The Idea of Human Equality," and "Christian Anti-Judaism." Dates before 1500 are shown with "c." where the chapter gives them as approximate. **Rules:** - The timeline runs from 300 CE to 2025, with four strands as horizontal lanes. - Each card has a fixed date and exactly one correct strand, given in Content. - Check is available when all 12 cards are placed; it scores all 12 at once. - After Check, correct cards lock; incorrect cards are marked and show the correct strand. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner reads the four strand definitions. 2. The learner drags each card, already set at its date, into a strand. 3. The learner presses Check; the score and feedback for each card appear. 4. The learner can then select any card to read its "Why" text. 5. The learner should notice that the three Luther cards (3, 4, 5) fall in three different strands, and that the contempt strand turns toward repudiation only after the Holocaust. **Feedback:** Twelve cards, placed in any order, one Check. Correct card: "Correct. [Why]" Incorrect card: "This one belongs in [correct strand]. [Why]" After Check: "[n] of 12 placed correctly. Mastery is 10." If n < 10, a "Try again" option returns all cards to the tray in the same order. A note appears after Check: "One man, Martin Luther, appears in three strands." **Starting State:** Four empty lanes on a timeline from 300 CE to 2025, the 12 cards in a tray in the fixed order, and the question "Which strand of Paul's legacy did each event carry forward?" **Chapter Anchors:** Augustine read Romans 13 in Milan in 386; Chrysostom's eight sermons, 386–387; 95 Theses, October 31, 1517; Worms, 1521; *On the Jews and Their Lies*, 1543; Wesley, May 24, 1738; *Slave Bible*, 1807; Stendahl, 1963; *Nostra Aetate*, 1965; Sanders, 1977; Dunn, 1982; *Joint Declaration*, 1999; twelve events; four strands.
